newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: 11 die in Pakistan sectarian, ethnic shootings.
newsitem.headline: 11 die in Pakistan sectarian, ethnic shootings.

text.p: At least 11 people were killed on Monday in apparent Moslem sectarian and ethnic shootings in Pakistan's central province of Punjab and the port city Karachi, government officials said.

Gunmen sprayed bullets in a bazaar in the southern Punjab town of Shorkot, killing at least seven people from the minority Shi'ite sect and one from the majority Sunni sect, a government official in the area said.
A Sunni lawyer, Mian Mohammad Arshad, and a Sunni banker, Waqar Ahmad Sheikh, were killed by gunmen in the provincial capital Lahore, police said.

In Karachi, unidentified gunmen killed a senior police officer, deputy superintendent Aslam Kayani, as a small ethnic party held protests for the second day running against the arrest of their workers, police said.
No one immediately claimed responsibility for the Punjab shootings but police said they seemed the latest in a wave of tit-for-tat attacks which militant Sunni and Shi'ite groups blame on each other.
The Karachi killing, which police blamed on "miscreants", followed the death of four people, including a three-year-old child, on Sunday in a renewed spate of violence in the city.
"A bullet pierced ... his (Kaysani's) heart when he came out of his vehicle to clear the road, which was blocked by the miscreants," Karachi police chief Mohammad Iqbal told Reuters.
Earlier, Shi'ite sources in Islamabad put the death toll in Shorkot at nine, saying all the victims were Shi'ites.

Sectarian violence is rife in Punjab with militant Sunni and Shi'ite factions engaged in a feud that officials say has killed more than 100 people so far this year, including religious scholars, lawyers and doctors.
On Sunday, a Shi'ite activist was shot by three men on motorcycles as he opened his shop in another Punjab town, Chichawatni, 200 km (125 miles) southwest of Lahore.
Sunni groups accuse neighbouring Shi'ite Iran of financing Pakistani Shi'ite militants, while Shi'ites accuse Sunni Saudi Arabia of aiding Sunni groups.

Sunni-Shi'ite disputes over Islamic beliefs have often spilled into violence in Pakistan. Shi'ites form about 15 percent of Pakistan's mainly Sunni population of more than 135 million but are the majority in Iran.
In Karachi, witnesses said parts of eastern Malir, Khorkarapar and Saudabad remained shut for the second day as supporters of the Mohajir National Movement (Haqiqi faction) held protests.
They set ablaze vehicles, burning old tyres to block transport and forcing shops and markets to close.
Police said armed youngsters fired shots in the air and tried to target the police vehicles.
Dozen of workers of Haqiqi have been detained in raids by police after the killing of another police officer on Friday.
The Haqiqi is a splinter faction of the main MQM, which renamed itself last week to Mutahidda (united) National Movement but retained the acronym MQM.
It speaks for the rights of Urdu-speaking people who migrated to Pakistan from India at partition in 1947 and their descendants.
More than 225 people have been killed in political violence in Karachi since March 1 compared to about 500 in 1996 and more than 2,000 in 1995.
